title: Vite, kjenne eller kunne — three kinds of knowing
goal: Choose vite for facts, kjenne for familiarity, and kunne for a learned skill or ability.

objectives.statement: Choose vite for facts, kjenne for familiarity, and kunne for a learned skill or ability.

sections.title: A first shift at the community centre

spans.value: Lea has recently moved to Trondheim. On Saturday she is helping at a neighbourhood event for the first time. Arne, one of the organisers, shows her around.

blocks.translation: Do you know where the kitchen is?

spans.value: Ja, det er i gangen til venstre. Men jeg kjenner ikke bygningen så godt ennå.

blocks.translation: Yes, it’s in the corridor on the left. But I don’t know the building very well yet.

spans.value: Kjenner du Mari? Hun har ansvaret for maten.

blocks.translation: Do you know Mari? She is in charge of the food.

spans.value: Nei, men jeg vet hvem hun er. Vi har ikke snakket sammen før.

blocks.translation: No, but I know who she is. We haven’t spoken before.

spans.value: Kan du lage kaffe med den store maskinen?

blocks.translation: Do you know how to make coffee with the large machine?

spans.value: Ja, jeg kan bruke en slik maskin. Jeg jobbet på kafé før.

blocks.translation: Yes, I know how to use that kind of machine. I used to work in a café.

spans.value: Flott. Vet du når gjestene kommer?

blocks.translation: Great. Do you know when the guests are coming?

spans.value: De kommer klokka to, tror jeg.

blocks.translation: They’re coming at two, I think.

sections.title: Kjenne: being familiar with someone or something

spans.value: when the point is familiarity gained through contact or experience. You may
a person because you have met and interacted with them. You may also
a city, neighbourhood, building, book, or type of situation because it is familiar to you.

en.value: Do you know Mari?

spans.value: He is not asking whether Lea has information about Mari. He wants to know whether Mari is personally familiar to her.

no.value: Nei, men jeg vet hvem hun er.

en.value: No, but I know who she is.
I know Mari.
I know who Mari is.

spans.value: The first sentence suggests personal familiarity. The second says only that the speaker knows Mari’s identity. You can know who someone is without knowing that person personally.
The same distinction appears with places.

en.value: I know Trondheim quite well.
I know where Trondheim is.

spans.value: In the first sentence, the speaker is familiar with the city. Perhaps they have lived there, visited often, or know their way around. In the second, the speaker knows a geographical fact.

en.value: Do you know the new neighbour?

no.value: Jeg kjenner ikke dette området så godt.

en.value: I don’t know this area very well.
She is already familiar with the restaurant.
We know her family well.

no.value: Han kjenner systemet etter mange år i firmaet.

en.value: He knows the system after many years at the company.

spans.value: often means to be familiar with something or to know of its existence.

en.value: Are you familiar with this author?

no.value: Jeg kjenner til problemet, men jeg vet ikke alle detaljene.

en.value: I am aware of the problem, but I don’t know all the details.

spans.value: Return to Lea’s first day at the community centre. Imagine she has seen Mari’s name on the schedule but has never spoken to her. Describe what Lea knows using one sentence about Mari’s identity and one sentence about personal familiarity.
This activity belongs here because the same person can be the subject of two different kinds of knowledge. A successful response demonstrates the difference between

sections.title: Kunne: having a learned skill or ability

spans.value: when someone has learned how to do something or has the ability to do it. Its present form is
At the community centre, Arne asks:

no.value: Kan du lage kaffe med den store maskinen?

en.value: Do you know how to make coffee with the large machine?

spans.value: Lea has used this type of machine before, so she answers:

no.value: Jeg kan bruke en slik maskin.

en.value: I know how to use that kind of machine.

spans.value: is normally followed by the infinitive without

en.value: I can swim.
She knows how to repair bicycles.
Do you know how to use this program?
He cannot drive.

spans.value: A language can also be treated as a learned ability.

en.value: Do you know Norwegian?
She knows a little Spanish.

spans.value: Keep the focus on an ability the person possesses. Compare factual knowledge with practical ability:

en.value: I know how the coffee machine works.
I know how to use the coffee machine.

spans.value: The first sentence concerns information about the machine’s operation. The second says that the speaker has the practical ability to operate it. Someone might understand how a machine works in theory but still be unable to use it confidently.

no.value: Emil vet hvordan man skifter et dekk.

en.value: Emil knows how to change a tyre.
Emil knows how to change a tyre.

spans.value: reports knowledge of the procedure. The sentence with
presents changing a tyre as Emil’s skill.

Use the event context again. Lea has read and understood the operating procedure for the sound system, but she has never operated it. Describe her factual knowledge of how the system works, then state whether the available context supports saying that she has the practical skill to use it.

The difference becomes clearer when all three verbs appear in similar questions.

en.value: Do you know who the pianist is?

spans.value: This asks for a fact: the pianist’s identity.

en.value: Do you know the pianist?
Can you play the piano?

spans.value: This asks about a learned skill.

en.value: Do you know where the swimming pool is?
Are you familiar with the swimming pool?
Can you swim?

spans.value: The first question asks for location information. The second asks whether the place is familiar. The third asks about an ability.

no.value: Vet du hva dette programmet heter?

en.value: Do you know what this program is called?
Are you familiar with this program?
Do you know how to use this program?

spans.value: These questions could all arise in one conversation, but they request different kinds of knowledge.

spans.value: For an ordinary neutral statement that someone has learned and can perform an action, normally use

spans.value: Assuming familiarity always includes detailed facts
Being familiar with something does not mean knowing every fact about it.

no.value: Jeg kjenner byen, men jeg vet ikke hvor det nye biblioteket er.

en.value: I know the city, but I don’t know where the new library is.

spans.value: Likewise, factual knowledge does not necessarily mean personal familiarity.

no.value: Jeg vet mye om forfatteren, men jeg kjenner henne ikke.

en.value: I know a lot about the author, but I don’t know her personally.

spans.value: Later that morning, after Mari, Lea, and Arne have spent time setting up rooms and talking together, Mari and Lea go into the kitchen to prepare coffee.
Hei, Lea. Nå har vi jobbet sammen en stund. Kjenner du Arne fra før?

blocks.translation: Hi, Lea. We’ve been working together for a while now. Did you know Arne before today?

spans.value: Nei, jeg møtte ham i dag. Men etter at vi har jobbet sammen, kjenner jeg både deg og Arne litt nå.

blocks.translation: No, I met him today. But after working together, I know both you and Arne a little now.

spans.value: Vet du hvor vi skal sette koppene?

blocks.translation: Do you know where we should put the cups?
Yes, Arne showed me the cupboard.

spans.value: Bra. Kan du også lage te med denne maskinen?

blocks.translation: Good. Do you also know how to make tea with this machine?

spans.value: Det kan jeg. Nå kjenner jeg kjøkkenet ganske godt også.

blocks.translation: I can do that. Now I know the kitchen quite well too.

This activity belongs here because it returns to the chapter’s people and situation while requiring the learner to choose independently among all three verbs. A successful response demonstrates that the learner can follow changes in context: spending time talking and working with a person can create personal familiarity, receiving information creates factual knowledge, and having learned a task supports a statement of ability.

explanation.value: Use vite for facts or information, kjenne for familiarity with people or places, and kunne for learned ability.

prompt.value: Write exactly two short sentences in Norwegian about Lea and Mari. The first sentence must say that Lea knows who Mari is because she has seen Mari’s name on the schedule. The second must say that Lea has no personal familiarity with Mari because they have never spoken. Keep identity and personal familiarity separate.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål variants that preserve the two meanings and the stated context. Pass only when identity and personal familiarity appear in separate sentences. A factual form such as «Jeg vet hvem Mari er.» and a familiarity form such as «Jeg kjenner ikke Mari.» are valid evidence.

criteria.instruction: States that Lea knows who Mari is, using a factual identity construction such as «Jeg vet hvem Mari er.»
States that Lea has no personal familiarity with Mari, using a natural form of kjenne such as «Jeg kjenner ikke Mari.»
Uses one sentence for identity and a different sentence for personal familiarity, so the two meanings are distinguished.

prompt.value: Write two short sentences in Norwegian about Lea and the sound system. In the first, state that she knows how the system works because she has read and understood the procedure. In the second, state whether the available context supports saying that she can operate it. Do not claim an ability that has not been established.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural variants such as «Hun vet hvordan lydanlegget fungerer, men vi vet ikke om hun kan bruke det.» The response must express factual knowledge of the procedure and uncertainty about operating ability. Reject both an unsupported positive claim that she can operate it and an unsupported claim that she cannot.

criteria.instruction: Uses vite hvordan to state Lea’s established knowledge of how the sound system works.
States that the context does not establish whether Lea can operate the system and does not assert that she has that ability.

prompt.value: Write twelve short Norwegian questions: three about each topic— a colleague, a town, a computer program, and a musical instrument. For every topic, ask one question about factual information, one about personal familiarity, and one about a learned ability. Keep the central topic constant within each trio; natural Norwegian may add a necessary complement for the ability question.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål wording, inflection, and necessary complements. Pass only when all four topics have three questions and each trio clearly contains factual information, personal familiarity, and learned ability. The response must use vet for factual questions, kjenner for familiarity, and kan for ability according to meaning, while keeping each topic central within its trio.

criteria.instruction: Keeps the colleague, town, computer program, and musical instrument as the central topics within their respective three-question groups.
Uses the present forms vet, kjenner, and kan for factual information, personal familiarity, and learned ability respectively in every topic group.

prompt.value: Write a short Norwegian message of four sentences about Lea after the community-centre event. Include a factual statement about where the cups go in the building, a familiarity statement about Mari and Arne after working together, a factual statement that Mari is on the work schedule, and an ability statement about making tea with the machine. Make the three kinds of knowing clear through your verb choices.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål variants that preserve all four requested details. Valid evidence can include «Jeg vet hvor vi skal sette koppene», «Jeg kjenner både Mari og Arne litt nå», «Jeg vet at Mari står på arbeidsplanen», and «Jeg kan lage te med denne maskinen». Check that factual information uses vite, familiarity uses kjenne, and practical ability uses kunne.

criteria.instruction: States a factual detail about where the cups belong in the building using a natural form of vite.
States that Lea is personally familiar with Mari and Arne after working together using a natural form of kjenne.
States the schedule information that Mari is on the work schedule using a natural factual form of vite.
States that Lea can make tea with the machine using a natural form of kunne, normally kan with an infinitive.

prompt.value: Write a short Norwegian exchange with one question-and-answer pair for each point. Ask or state the hotel’s location or address as factual information, ask or state whether one friend is familiar with Bergen, and ask or state whether the other friend has the learned ability to drive confidently in heavy traffic. Keep location, familiarity, and driving ability separate.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål alternatives that preserve the three roles. Pass when hotel location or address is expressed as factual knowledge with vite, Bergen familiarity with kjenne, and learned driving ability with kan plus an infinitive. Do not accept a response that treats familiarity or driving skill as the hotel-location fact.

criteria.instruction: Keeps the hotel’s location or address as factual information and uses a natural form of vite for it.
Uses a natural form of kjenne to express personal familiarity with Bergen.
Uses a natural form of kan with a driving infinitive to express learned driving ability, separately from location and familiarity.

prompt.value: Write a brief Norwegian exchange in which one organiser asks another organiser about all three kinds of knowledge. Include a question and reply about the concert’s starting time, a question and reply about personal acquaintance with the singer, and a question and reply about the ability to use the sound equipment.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept natural Bokmål exchanges with equivalent wording. Pass only when the starting time is treated as a fact with vet, the singer as a personally known person with kjenner, and operating the equipment as a learned ability with kan plus an appropriate infinitive such as bruke.

criteria.instruction: Uses a natural form of vet for the concert’s starting-time information.
Uses a natural form of kjenner to express personal acquaintance with the singer.
Uses a natural form of kan plus an infinitive to express the ability to use the sound equipment.

prompt.value: Choose one coherent situation that supports all three kinds of knowledge. Write three short Norwegian statements: one fact someone knows, one person or place someone is familiar with, and one learned skill someone possesses. Then write a brief Norwegian explanation for each statement, explaining why it requires vite, kjenne, or kunne.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept any coherent situation and natural Bokmål wording. Pass only when the response contains one concrete factual statement, one personal or place familiarity statement, and one learned-skill statement, followed by a separate explanation for each choice. The explanations must connect fact to vite, familiarity to kjenne, and ability to kunne; a bare list without explanations is insufficient.

criteria.instruction: States one concrete fact someone knows using a natural present form of vite, such as vet.
Names a person or place someone is familiar with using a natural present form of kjenne, such as kjenner.
States one learned skill someone possesses using a natural present form of kunne, such as kan with an infinitive.
Explains separately in Norwegian why each of the three statements requires vite, kjenne, or kunne according to its meaning.
